name: How much contingency should you set aside for a gut renovation?

mainEntity.name: What contingency budget is smart for a gut renovation in Los Angeles or Pasadena?
mainEntity.text: What contingency budget is smart for a gut renovation in Los Angeles or Pasadena?

acceptedAnswer.text: A contingency is not optional on a gut renovation, especially in older Los Angeles-area homes. Once demolition begins, it is common to discover issues that were not visible during the estimate phase. A practical planning range is often 10% to 20% of the construction budget, with higher reserves sometimes needed for historic homes, hillside properties, or projects involving custom structural work. The exact amount should reflect the age of the house, the completeness of preconstruction inspection, and how much of the home is being rebuilt. Homeowners should also separate contingency from design upgrades, because many budgets fail when change orders and nicer selections are mixed together. A strong contract should explain how contingency is held, who can approve it, and what qualifies as an unforeseen condition versus a homeowner-driven upgrade.
acceptedAnswer.description: A gut renovation should include a contingency because demolition often reveals hidden structural, mechanical, or moisture damage. A common planning range is at least 10% to 20% of construction cost, with older homes or luxury projects sometimes needing more. Lower contingencies can leave projects underfunded.
